source_review.notes: Checked all six references at the RFC Editor or NIST. RFC 6749 defines scope request and granted-scope behavior; RFC 9700 requires minimum-privilege access tokens and recommends audience plus action restriction; RFC 8707 defines resource indicators and audience-restricted tokens; RFC 9396 defines typed authorization_details; RFC 9068 defines JWT access-token claims including aud and scope; NIST SP 800-162 supplies the ABAC vocabulary and current-policy context. The chapter distinguishes normative protocol behavior from local design guidance.

evidence: Reviewed requested Q(q), client C(c), actor U(u), resource R(r), grant G(g), restriction P(p), effective E, token-validity V_token, and local authorization A symbols for consistent definitions.
Corrected the subset statement so E is explicitly a subset of each input set rather than an ambiguous comma-separated expression.
Confirmed the equations use GitHub-compatible math delimiters and the code vocabulary matches the prose intersection model.
notation_and_syntax.notes: The notation cleanly separates token-minting set intersection from current object/action authorization.

numerical_recomputation.notes: No probability, cost, rate, latency, benchmark, or other quantitative claim requires numerical recomputation.

evidence: Re-derived E = Q(q) intersection C(c) intersection U(u) intersection R(r) intersection G(g) intersection P(p), which guarantees E is a subset of every authority source.
Re-derived allow(x,o) as token validity AND required-action membership in E AND current local authorization A, confirming scope is necessary but not sufficient.
Checked that downscoping by further intersection cannot add permissions and that composite expansion must occur before the governed intersection.
symbolic_recomputation.notes: The algebra establishes non-expansion only when every input set is authoritative; the chapter explicitly states that limitation.

evidence: Reviewed empty, omitted, excessive, unknown, wildcard, composite, negative, multi-audience, exchanged, refreshed, revoked, user, service, and delegated grant cases.

Reviewed wrong audience, cross-tenant/object access, disallowed state, property-level mutation, batch/filter expansion, GraphQL resolver, async job, WebSocket, event, internal-call, and support-tool bypasses.

Reviewed legacy broad-scope migration, newly introduced destructive actions, stale role/group mapping, policy-cache outage, emergency disable, disclosure through errors, and leaked bearer-token replay.
boundary_and_adversarial_cases.notes: The adversarial analysis covers over-issuance, over-use, alternate entry paths, semantic drift, and delayed restriction propagation.

evidence: Executed effective-permission-intersection: only orders.cancel and orders.read were granted from the five intersected inputs.
Confirmed own open cancellation allowed while another owner's order, a shipped order, missing refund permission, and wrong audience were independently denied.
Checked the prose and exercises preserve minimal defaults, audience restriction, frozen composite meaning, explicit local policy, and non-expanding downscope invariants.
invariant_checking.notes: The deterministic model demonstrates the central invariants but intentionally omits OAuth message and cryptographic token validation.

proof_review.notes: No formal authorization, protocol-composition, cryptographic, or policy-completeness proof is claimed.

evidence: Confirmed the set-intersection result is presented as a bounded non-expansion argument, not proof that its inputs or enforcement coverage are correct.
Confirmed standards requirements, design recommendations, implementation examples, migration guidance, and remaining operational obligations are distinguished.
proof_sketch_labeling.notes: The chapter explicitly says wrong, stale, attacker-controlled, or incorrectly mapped source sets can still make E unsafe.

evidence: Snippet report artifacts/snippets/API-045/report.json records one passing deterministic local permission-intersection and authorization execution.
Production issuer, resource server, policy store, consent UI, token exchange, revocation, performance, and attack tests are listed as verification obligations rather than completed measurements.
empirical_evidence_labeling.notes: No live authorization deployment, penetration test, latency measurement, or grant inventory was empirically assessed.

conceptual_review.notes: Reviewed the separation of audience, permission, actor/client/grant, and object/state policy; task-derived permission vocabulary; atomic/composite semantics; minimal defaults; rich authorization details; role mapping; enforcement coverage; lifecycle; errors; observability; and migration as one coherent least-privilege model.

practitioner_review.notes: Checked deployability through a permission registry, resource-specific token issuance, closed authorization-detail schemas, gateway-plus-service enforcement, route/schema coverage tests, safe denial telemetry, emergency disable, grant/token inventory, dual-read migration, bounded refresh behavior, and rollback that never silently broadens authority. Product-specific vocabulary and risk thresholds remain governed configuration.

pedagogical_review.notes: The chapter starts with the intersection and local-policy distinction, then builds permission derivation, granularity, resource restriction, structured authorization, enforcement, governance, and verification. Ten examples isolate common design decisions; five exercises synthesize catalogue design, set computation, rich authorization, path coverage, and migration with detailed answers.

limitations: Internal evidence record only; no external academic or practitioner review is claimed.
